native_result.query: In which domain do the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies?
native_result.HypoA: In Experimental Economics, the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies with ratio of males in original and replication studies being and 0.87 and 0.84 respectively.
native_result.HypoB: Economics is the domain in which the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies: 77.8% of Economics original/replication pairs have majority-male original author teams (mean male ratio 0.870) and 72.2% have majority-male replication teams (mean male ratio 0.837), the only discipline satisfying the majority condition on both sides, whereas Cognitive (0.711 original vs 0.521 replication) and Social psychology (0.658 vs 0.495) are majority-male among originals but not among replications, whose large multi-lab teams approach gender parity.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded the study-level CSV (927 lab-level rows, 141 unique O/R pairs; 927 rows, zero missingness in key fields; confirmed authors_male coding as male-author ratio via integer product check). Built a pair-level table (originals: constant per id; replications: aggregated row for ml1/ml3, single row for rpp/ee). Computed per discipline: mean male ratio, share of pairs with authors_male > 0.5, and share majority-male on both sides, for original and replication sides, plus author-weighted ratios. Robustness: (1) re-ran excluding drop=True pairs — results unchanged; (2) pooled multi-lab replication teams (lab-level authors_male.r averaged per pair and lab-team-level shares) — Economics still 0.778/0.722, Cognitive/Social replication sides remain below 0.55; (3) verified the second CSV lacks author-gender/discipline data and was excluded; (4) treated replication author-weighted counts as approximate (96 non-integer rows). Economics results are reported with their single-project (ee) composition and not generalized across projects.
